E0283.summary: Nature's outer level, where things appear varied and nothing homogeneous is seen, as opposed to the root.
E0283.body: Atwood uses *circumference* for nature's outer level, where things appear varied and nothing homogeneous is seen, in contrast to the root: “For nature at the circumference subsists in this way” [III.4 ¶8].

E0284.summary: The outward life of the spirit, terrified at first by the new light and contrasted with its 'central whole'.
E0284.body: In Atwood's notes, the *circumferential life* is the outward life of the spirit. The new light at first “causes a terrification of the whole circumferential life” [I.3 n69]. It is set against a central whole, into which the spirit is spoken of as “converting her circumferential manifestations into their central whole conditionedly” [I.3 n65]. The context suggests the outward manifestations are to be drawn back into the centre.

E0285.summary: In a passage quoted from Hermes, a stage or substance extracted out of the Red, from which Botri is made.
E0285.body: In the passage quoted from Hermes, Citrine is extracted out of the Red, and Botri is made from it: “if it be citrine and nothing else know it will be thy Wisdom” [I.3 ¶41]. The text does not explain it further.

E0286.summary: According to Flammel, as reported through Eudoxus, the Mercury used for the Imbibition of the Red.
E0286.body: Eudoxus reports Flammel as saying that “one must make use of the citrine Mercury to make the Imbibition of the Red” [IV.3 ¶10]. The text does not explain it further.

E0287.summary: In the Appendix, the intermediate state through which present life is led into the third life.
E0287.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood describes the clairvoyant life as the intermediate state through which present life passes into the third life: “this present life may be led through the clairvoyant life into it” [APP ¶2]. Compare *common trance*, in which the third life is not known.

E0288.summary: Atwood's term for the purified substance on which all Forms arise spontaneously, as the true Genesis of Light.
E0288.body: Atwood speaks of a purified substance on which all Forms arise spontaneously, as the true Genesis of Light: “this clarified hypostasis (shall we not believe in it?), is the stage of all Forms” [III.2 ¶26]. Elsewhere in the same chapter she uses *hypostasis* for the ground that bounds abstract reason; met by the inner light, that ground is the Absolute Identity [III.2 ¶31]. The text does not say that these two uses name the same thing, so both readings are open.

E0289.summary: Author of De Raptu Prosepinae, which Atwood quotes to illustrate entry into the arcane mysteries and the advent of the deity at Eleusis.
E0289.body: Atwood quotes Claudian's work (spelled *de Paptu Proserpineae* / *De Raptu Prosepinae* in the text) to illustrate entry into the arcane mysteries and the advent of the deity at Eleusis: “Jam furor humanus nostro de pectore sensus Expluit” [II.3 ¶15; II.3 ¶19; II.3 n11; II.3 n14]. She uses him as supporting illustration.

E0290.summary: Writer Atwood cites for the books of Hermes and as a witness that the Mysteries were sacred and continued in Christianity.
E0290.body: Atwood cites Clemens Alexandrinus as naming in detail the books attributed to Hermes [I.1 ¶7]. She uses him in support of her view of the Mysteries. He called them blessed: “O mysteries truly sacred, O pure light!” He also describes the Greater Mysteries as unveiling nature, with the Lord as hierophant [II.2 ¶3; II.2 ¶5; II.2 n9]. In Part IV, “the Bishop of Alexandria” is cited, with a footnote naming Clemens Alexandrinus, for the view that the Mysteries continued in Christianity, the Lord illuminating the Adepts: “It is the Lord himself who is the Hierophanta.” [IV.2 ¶16; IV.2 n12]. The link to the footnote depends on reading the marker (2) as n12.

E0291.summary: Cited to illustrate the art's revival in Egypt, through her earring dissolved in philosophic vinegar and the chemical treatises attributed to her.
E0291.body: Atwood mentions Cleopatra when describing the art's revival in Egypt. She cites the earring dissolved in philosophic vinegar and the chemical treatises attributed to Cleopatra, including *Ars auri faciendi* [I.1 ¶18; I.1 n25].

E0292.summary: In the poem The Hunting of the Greene Lyon, the learned person who will find truth in the work, as against the 'lay'.
E0292.body: In the quoted poem *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon*, the *Clerke* is the learned person who will find truth in the work: “For surely if thow be a Clerke, Thow wilt finde trewth in thys werke:” [III.1 ¶65]. The lay are told to keep counsel and leave off. The narrator says he is “noe Clerke” in science, yet he has laboured in the work.

E0293.summary: Something the depraved 'entangled' and climbed by into self-sufficiency; not explained in the text.
E0293.body: Atwood says the depraved climbed into self-sufficiency “basely entangling the clue of life” [III.4 ¶4]. The text does not explain the expression further.

E0294.summary: A spirit born with us, whose use the initiated lose on seeing the Divine Nature; the vision in Hades is allied to it.
E0294.body: Atwood describes a spirit born with us, whose use the initiated lose when they see the Divine Nature: “For to this spirit the vision in Hades is allied” [II.4 ¶19].

E0295.summary: The error of treating the Identity of Being as heaped up or compounded instead of uncompounded.
E0295.body: Atwood warns that “the Identity of every Being is something uncompounded, and that the mind should not fall into the error of coacervation” [III.2 ¶52]. Coacervation is thus the error of treating that Identity as heaped up or compounded. Compare *compounded*.

E0296.summary: Fixing or setting, alternated with dissolution; Albertus says the cleansed Argent vive is coagulated by its own internal sulfur.
E0296.body: In the passage quoted from Albertus, coagulation is fixing or setting, alternated with dissolution: “a successive dissolution and coagulation to make the fixed volatile, and volatile fixed” [IV.1 ¶4]. The cleansed Argent vive is coagulated by its own internal sulfur. Synesius lists *coagulate* among the names of the one operation of coction (see *coction*).

E0297.summary: In a passage from Hermes, a coal whose life is fire; extinct, it becomes a dead body and is returned to the water for thirty days.
E0297.body: In the passage quoted from Hermes: “The life of the coal is fire, which being extinct, becomes a dead body” [I.3 n22]. The extinct coal is returned to the water for thirty days. The text gives no plain meaning.

E0298.summary: The cooking or maturing of the matter; Synesius says all the named operations are only names for this single operation.
E0298.body:
Coction is the cooking, digesting or maturing of the matter.

- **Atwood** speaks of the elixir obtained “through superior skill and coction in the vegetal life” [I.2 ¶46].
- **Basil Valentine** calls it the boiling and maturing of the stone of Fire with the corporeal fire of the microcosm: “let no man wonder at this coction” [III.1 ¶37].
- **During the severation**, Atwood writes, “a wonderful coction is described as going on” [III.1 ¶53]. The waters decoct the sensual dominant, and the dragons are decocted in their own venom.
- **Synesius** describes a gentle, gradual and long cooking, “the coction of this water”. He treats it as the single operation: dissolve, calcine, tinge, whiten, renew, bathe, wash, coagulate, imbibe, fix, grind, dry and distill “are all one, and signify no more than to decoct nature until such time as she be perfected” [III.3 ¶60].
- **Decoction**, Atwood reports, is what Hermes calls the first part of the work: “the former Hermes calls decoction, which dissolving the matter discharges also its impurities by a proper rule” [I.3 n7]. It reduces the matter until it is close to annihilation and free of every outward form.
- **Zachary** treats the cooking as continuing until it is complete: “donec decoctio compleatur” (ours: until the decoction is completed) [IV.1 ¶9].

E0300.summary: In a passage from Hermes, named as one of several substances that are also sulphur.
E0300.body: In the passage quoted from Hermes, colcothar is named as a kind of sulphur: “the auripigment, siretz, and colcothar, which are also sulphur” [I.3 ¶20].

E0301.summary: In Iamblicus, the first class of prayer, belonging to the early initiations and pertaining to Illumination.
E0301.body: Iamblicus, as quoted, calls the first class of prayer, belonging to the early initiations, Collective. It pertains to Illumination and “was called Collective, having for its object to gather the mental powers into accord with their leader” [III.4 ¶24]. Compare *Communion of Operation*, the second class.

E0302.summary: The stages of colour the work passes through; in Hermes' division of the Water, colour is a third part, a coagulating moisture.
E0302.body: The colours are the stages the work must pass through. In Hermes' division of the Water, colour is one third part: “the one third part of which is colour, that is to say --- a coagulating moisture” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast says Hermes divides the colours “into three red spirits and three white, which have their growth all from the same identical water” [I.3 n5].

E0303.summary: In Norton's Ordinal, a mixing-in of something, to be avoided.
E0303.body: Norton's Ordinal warns: “Beware of Commixtion that nothing miscape.” [IV.1 ¶28]. Commixtion is a mixing-in of something that must be avoided.

E0304.summary: For Atwood, the agent at work in present-day mesmerism and also the Alchemists' subject-matter: indifferent, present everywhere and converted to every will.
E0304.body: Atwood identifies the Common Soul with “the identical agent which is spread abroad in the present day mesmerizing, the photogenic medium, our New Imponderable, for it is the Common Soul”. She says it is “also the subject-matter of the Alchemists aforesaid” [II.2 ¶18]. It is indifferent, present everywhere and converted to every will: “a thing indifferent, abject, and exposed in all hands” [II.2 ¶18]. This is a central identity for her method: the mesmeric agent and the alchemical matter are one.

E0305.summary: In the Appendix, the entranced life of sleep-walkers, produced by fermenting present life by its similar; the third life is not known in it.
E0305.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says that fermenting present life by its similar “leads into the common trance, or is entranced” [APP ¶3]. She equates the common trance with “the common entranced life, i.e., the life of the sleep-walkers” [APP ¶2]. The third life is not known in it. Compare *clairvoyant life*.

E0306.summary: The connection the work requires; it is disturbed by air currents, and communion with superiors needs a heavenly way of life.
E0306.body: Atwood says that “Strong currents of air are well known to disturb communion” [III.4 ¶42]. She also warns that a heavenly way of life is needed, “otherwise thou canst have no communion with superiors” [III.4 ¶44].

E0307.summary: In Iamblicus, what the second class of prayer pertains to; it effects the bonds of concordant spirits.
E0307.body: Iamblicus, as quoted, says that the second class of prayer pertains to a Communion of Operation: “the second, to a Communion of Operation” [III.4 ¶24]. This class effects the bonds of concordant spirits before intellectual alliance. Compare *Collective*.

E0308.summary: In Vaughan, what is to be sought where extremes meet; not further defined.
E0308.body: Vaughan, as quoted, advises: “where extremes meet, there look for complexions” [III.4 ¶44]. The text does not define the term further.

E0309.summary: In Eudoxus, the compound the Wise man makes by secret union of the fixed with the volatile; Geber's mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur.
E0309.body: Eudoxus says of the compound of Art: “it is the Wise man who makes it by the secret union of the fixed with the volatile” [IV.3 ¶9]. It is always made by the Artist and is not altogether the same in the Second and Third Work. He adds: “Geber defines it, a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶9]. Compare *compound of Nature*.

E0310.summary: In Eudoxus, the compound treated in the First Key, made by Nature in ways the Artist cannot understand; he only aids her by external things.
E0310.body: Eudoxus says: “The first is the compound of Nature, whereof I have spoken in the First Key” [IV.3 ¶9]. Nature makes it in a way the Artist cannot understand, and he only aids her by external things. Compare *compound of Art*.

E0311.summary: Atwood's term for the art's matter: one essence containing everything yet separated in each particular, the ground of the magians' elements.
E0311.body: Atwood calls the art's matter “the compound simple of this art”. The hen's egg corresponds to it, except in catholicity [I.3 n26]. In Part II she describes it as “an essence all comprehending, yet separated in each particular, by so great an interval from itself” [II.2 ¶19]. She identifies it with the Monster and the Eternal Riddle: “This is the Monster and the Eternal Riddle explained to common sense as suits it, but misunderstood to this day; that Compound Simple”. She also calls it the ground of the elements: “that Compound Simple and ground of the magians’ elements” [II.2 ¶19].

E0312.summary: Whatever is mixed or impure; it cannot approach the divine Fire, which destroys and separates it.
E0312.body: In a passage drawing on Sendivogius, *compounded* means whatever is mixed or impure: “nothing that is filthy or compounded, or blemished may come near Him” [II.4 ¶39]. The divine Fire destroys and separates what is compounded. It is unclear whether this view is Atwood's own or reported from Sendivogius; the records tag both voices. Compare *coacervation*.

E0313.summary: In Iamblichus, contributing causes: the soul's best dispositions and purity, which accompany the work without being its principal cause.
E0313.body: Iamblichus, as quoted, names “all the best dispositions of the soul, and also the purity pertaining, as certain concauses” [II.4 ¶31]. They are contributing causes that accompany the work without being its principal cause.
